body:
Meaning and historical background

Socio-religious reform refers to efforts to change social customs and religious practices that reformers considered unjust, harmful or unreasonable. In nineteenth-century Gujarat, reformers questioned caste discrimination, restrictions on women's education, opposition to widow remarriage, child marriage and beliefs associated with witchcraft and supernatural powers.

Religious and social questions were closely connected. A belief about ritual purity, for example, could be used to justify restrictions on eating together or crossing the sea. A customary understanding of marriage could prevent a widow from remarrying. Reformers therefore debated both the religious arguments used to defend customs and their effects on everyday life.

Gujarat's reform movement developed within the wider changes taking place in western India under colonial rule. New schools, printed books, newspapers and opportunities for discussion allowed educated Indians to question established practices. Many reformers wrote and spoke in Gujarati so that their ideas could reach people beyond those educated in English.

Three main methods of reform

Reformers and rulers used different methods. These methods sometimes supported one another, but they were not identical.

  • Public meetings and reform associations: Groups discussed religious beliefs and social customs, attempted to persuade people and created support for change. The Manav Dharma Sabha, established at Surat in 1844, is an early example.
  • Education and Gujarati-language publications: Schools, books, essays and periodicals encouraged the spread of useful knowledge and public criticism of harmful practices. The Gujarat Vernacular Society, established at Ahmedabad in 1848, and Narmad's periodical Dandiyo, launched in 1864, illustrate this approach.
  • State-supported education and legislation: A ruler could use governmental authority to introduce schools and laws. In Baroda State, Sayajirao Gaekwad III experimented with compulsory primary education in the Amreli area in 1893 and extended it throughout the state in 1906.

Why the regional setting matters

Surat, Ahmedabad, Bombay and Baroda were important centres, but they did not have identical political arrangements. Surat and Ahmedabad were within British-administered territories, while Baroda was a princely state ruled by the Gaekwads. Bombay, now Mumbai, was an important centre of Gujarati intellectual and publishing activity.

This distinction matters when studying reform laws. A measure introduced by Sayajirao in Baroda State did not automatically apply to every part of Gujarat. Similarly, a voluntary society could advocate widow remarriage without having the authority to change the law.

Social reform was gradual and contested. The establishment of a society, publication of an essay or passage of a law did not mean that established customs disappeared immediately. Reformers frequently faced opposition from conservative sections of society.

The main figures

The leading personalities in this lesson represent different but related approaches. Durgaram Mehta helped establish an early reform association; Dalpatram used poetry and educational institutions; Narmad used public criticism and Gujarati writing; Mahipatram Rupram Nilkanth promoted education and organized reform; and Sayajirao Gaekwad III employed the authority of Baroda State.

Prelims focus

  • 1844: Manav Dharma Sabha was established at Surat.
  • 1848: Gujarat Vernacular Society was established at Ahmedabad.
  • 1864: Narmad and his associates launched Dandiyo.
  • 1893 and 1906: Important stages in compulsory primary education under Sayajirao Gaekwad III.
  • Trap: A reform association, a periodical and a princely-state law are different types of historical developments.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 94–100; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Print Culture and the Modern World, printed pp. 168–171; Gujarati Vishwakosh, article Gujarat (History), nineteenth-century reform section, consulted 20 November 2026.]

body:
Durgaram Mehta as an early reformer

Durgaram Manchharam Mehta (1809–1876), commonly called Durgaram Mehtaji, was an early social reformer and teacher associated with Surat. He believed that social customs should be examined through moral reasoning rather than accepted merely because they were old or widely followed.

His work was important because it helped turn individual criticism of established customs into organized public discussion. The issues raised in Surat influenced the wider reform atmosphere of nineteenth-century Gujarat.

Foundation of the Manav Dharma Sabha

The Manav Dharma Sabha was established at Surat on 22 June 1844 by Durgaram and his reform-minded associates, including Dadoba Pandurang. It was among the earliest organized socio-religious reform associations in Gujarat.

The expression Manav Dharma conveys the idea of a moral religion concerned with human conduct. The Sabha maintained that religious practice should be judged by truth, ethical behaviour and reason, rather than by superstition or inherited social privilege.

Principal ideas

  • Belief in one God: The Sabha accepted monotheism and questioned forms of religious practice that its members regarded as inconsistent with this belief.
  • Opposition to caste discrimination: It questioned the assumption that a person's worth or moral status was determined by birth.
  • Support for widow remarriage: Durgaram challenged the restrictions that prevented widows from remarrying and argued for improvement in their social condition.
  • Criticism of superstition: The Sabha opposed beliefs and practices involving witchcraft, black magic, ghosts and similar supernatural claims.
  • Moral improvement: Its members encouraged people to examine their conduct and social customs through discussion.

The Sabha held regular Sunday meetings in which such questions were discussed. Public discussion was significant because it allowed reformers to challenge accepted ideas in front of an audience rather than through private conversation alone.

Its influence and limitations

Members of the Sabha challenged social conventions that enjoyed considerable support. They encountered opposition, especially over caste distinctions and widow remarriage. The Sabha itself was short-lived. Dadoba Pandurang was transferred to Bombay in 1846, and Durgaram subsequently moved away from Surat; its organized activity weakened around the early 1850s.

Its importance lies less in the length of its existence than in its example: a local group could meet openly, question superstition, discuss women's position and promote social equality. Later reformers in Gujarat continued to address many of these questions through literature, educational activity and other associations.

Manav Dharma Sabha was a reform association, not a government department. Its main instruments were discussion, moral argument and persuasion. Its objectives should not be confused with legislation enacted by a ruler.

Prelims focus

  • Durgaram Manchharam Mehta lived from 1809 to 1876.
  • Manav Dharma Sabha: Surat, 22 June 1844.
  • Dadoba Pandurang: An associate in its establishment.
  • The Sabha emphasized monotheism, criticism of caste discrimination, widow remarriage and opposition to superstition.
  • The departures of leading associates contributed to the decline of its activities.
  • Trap: Manav Dharma Sabha of 1844 was not the Prarthana Samaj established in Bombay in 1867.

[Sources: Gujarati Vishwakosh, articles Mehtaji, Durgaram and Gujarat (History), sections on Durgaram Mehta and Manav Dharma Sabha, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The Manav Dharma Sabha used religious and ethical principles in public discussion to criticize caste discrimination, widow remarriage restrictions and superstition.
pictures.caption: The Sabha connected religious reasoning with practical social reform.

title: Durgaram Mehta and the Manav Dharma Sabha of Surat

body:
Dalpatram's contribution to social change

Dalpatram Dahyabhai Travadi (1820–1898) was a Gujarati poet, prose writer and social reformer born at Wadhwan in Saurashtra. His writings communicated social criticism through familiar language, poetry, humour and examples drawn from everyday life.

Dalpatram commonly favoured gradual reform. He sought to persuade readers and listeners that education, useful knowledge and the rejection of harmful customs would benefit society. His association with Alexander Kinloch Forbes, a British official interested in Gujarati language and history, gave him an important institutional role.

Establishment of the Gujarat Vernacular Society

The Gujarat Vernacular Society was established in Ahmedabad on 26 December 1848 through the initiative of Alexander Kinloch Forbes and his associates, with Dalpatram's assistance. Dalpatram later worked as an assistant secretary of the Society.

The word vernacular refers here to the language commonly used by the people of the region. The Society aimed to promote Gujarati language and literature, spread useful knowledge and improve education. It helped make printed learning material more accessible to Gujarati readers.

Main activities

  • Promoting books and educational writing in Gujarati.
  • Supporting libraries and the collection of manuscripts.
  • Encouraging schooling, including education for girls.
  • Publishing newspapers and periodicals that circulated information and ideas.

The Society started the Gujarati weekly Vartaman in 1849. Because it appeared on Wednesdays, it also became known as Budhvariyu. The Society later took responsibility for the monthly periodical Buddhiprakash, which developed into an important medium for Gujarati educational and literary discussion. The monthly publication is associated with 1854, and Dalpatram became its editor in 1855.

The Gujarat Vernacular Society subsequently became known as Gujarat Vidya Sabha. The later name should not be mistaken for an entirely unrelated nineteenth-century institution.

Dalpatram's important writings

WorkYearMain relevance
Bhoot Nibandh1849An essay examining popular beliefs about ghosts and superstitions.
Hunnarkhan ni Chadhai1851A poetic address encouraging useful skills, crafts and industry.
Mithyabhiman1871A satirical play exposing false pride and social pretensions.

Bhoot Nibandh addressed beliefs that could encourage fear or irrational behaviour. Its significance was the attempt to examine prevailing ideas through reason and discussion.

Hunnarkhan ni Chadhai linked social improvement with practical work and economic progress. It encouraged people to value useful occupations, craftsmanship and productive activity.

Mithyabhiman used satire to criticize exaggerated pride and conventional attitudes. Its method illustrates how literature could encourage social reflection without taking the form of a formal religious debate.

Founding and association are different facts. Alexander Kinloch Forbes was the principal initiator of the Gujarat Vernacular Society. Dalpatram was a significant collaborator and later office-bearer; describing him as its sole founder would be inaccurate.

Prelims focus

  • Dalpatram: 1820–1898; born at Wadhwan.
  • Gujarat Vernacular Society: Ahmedabad, 26 December 1848; associated with Forbes and Dalpatram.
  • Vartaman: Gujarati weekly started in 1849.
  • Buddhiprakash: Gujarati periodical; Dalpatram became editor in 1855.
  • Bhoot Nibandh: 1849; concerned popular beliefs and superstitions.
  • Trap: Buddhiprakash was a periodical, while the Gujarat Vernacular Society was an organization.

[Sources: Gujarati Vishwakosh, articles Kavi Dalpatram, Gujarat Vidya Sabha (Gujarat Vernacular Society) and Buddhiprakash, consulted 20 November 2026; Maharashtra State Gazetteers, Language and Literature, section on Dalpatram Dahyabhai, consulted 20 November 2026.]

body:
Narmad and his reformist outlook

Narmadashankar Lalshankar Dave (1833–1886), widely known as Narmad, was a poet, prose writer and social reformer born in Surat. He became an influential figure in modern Gujarati literature and public debate.

Narmad believed that literature should do more than entertain readers. It could also challenge established customs, encourage education and develop a sense of collective identity. His writings connected social reform with the growing use of Gujarati as a language of public discussion.

Social practices challenged by Narmad

Narmad argued for women's education and supported widow remarriage. He opposed caste-based restrictions and questioned customs that prevented individuals from exercising freedom of thought and action.

His reformist language was often direct and critical. Rather than limiting himself to the position that education was desirable, he challenged the attitudes and institutions that obstructed it. This made his public interventions distinctive, though his efforts formed part of a wider movement that included other writers and social organizations.

Dandiyo and reform journalism

Dandiyo was a reform-oriented Gujarati periodical launched by Narmad and his associates on 1 September 1864. It initially appeared as a fortnightly publication and later became a weekly in 1868.

Its articles criticized hypocrisy, social abuses and conservative attitudes. The periodical provided a forum for debate about public conduct and the need for change. It was produced principally in Bombay, demonstrating that Gujarati reform activity extended beyond the geographical limits of present-day Gujarat.

A newspaper or periodical could influence readers by making arguments available for repeated discussion. Unlike a meeting, which required people to gather at a particular place and time, a printed article could circulate among readers and be read aloud to others. This was one reason Gujarati journalism became important to the reform movement.

Important literary works and their significance

  • Narmakosh: A Gujarati dictionary completed in 1873. It contributed to the development and organization of the Gujarati language.
  • Mari Hakikat: Narmad's autobiography, composed in 1866. It is an important early example of autobiographical writing in Gujarati.
  • Jai Jai Garavi Gujarat: A well-known poem expressing pride in Gujarat. It is associated with Narmad's contribution to regional consciousness.
  • Narmagadya: A collection associated with his development of modern Gujarati prose and reformist writing.

Narmad's activities show how social criticism and language development could reinforce one another. A growing body of Gujarati prose and journalism made it easier to discuss public issues in a shared language.

Association with reform circles

Narmad was connected with the intellectual and reform activities of the Buddhivardhak Hindu Sabha in Bombay, an association active from 1851. Discussions connected with this circle addressed subjects such as women's education, widow remarriage and social improvement.

It is important to distinguish the Sabha from publications with similar-sounding names. Buddhivardhak Hindu Sabha was an association; Buddhiprakash was a Gujarati periodical connected with the Gujarat Vernacular Society; and Dandiyo was Narmad's reform-oriented periodical.

Dalpatram and Narmad both contributed to Gujarati-language reform, but their methods differed in emphasis. Dalpatram frequently used gradual persuasion, poetry and institutional educational work; Narmad was especially noted for outspoken prose, journalism and direct public criticism. Neither should be reduced to a single literary genre.

Prelims focus

  • Narmad: 1833–1886; born in Surat.
  • Dandiyo: Launched on 1 September 1864 as a fortnightly Gujarati periodical.
  • Narmakosh: Gujarati dictionary completed in 1873.
  • Mari Hakikat: Narmad's autobiography.
  • Jai Jai Garavi Gujarat: Associated with Narmad.
  • Trap: Dandiyo, Buddhiprakash and Buddhivardhak Hindu Sabha are not names for the same institution.

[Sources: Gujarati Vishwakosh, articles Narmad, Dandiyo and Gujarat (History), consulted 20 November 2026; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Print Culture and the Modern World, printed pp. 169–171; The Wire, An Account of 19th-Century Western India in Narmadashankar Dave's Autobiography, 2025, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Narmad: Social Reform, Gujarati Journalism and Regional Consciousness
